title: Decidability of fifth-order \(\beta\)-matching
formal: Is fifth-order \(\beta\)-matching decidable in the source's closed range formulation? Given finite simple types \(\sigma,\tau\) and closed simply typed lambda terms \(F:\sigma\to\tau\) and \(N:\tau\), with \(\operatorname{ord}(\sigma)\le5\), decide whether \[\exists M\;\bigl(\varnothing\vdash M:\sigma\ \land\ F\,M=_\beta N\bigr).\] The unknown \(M\) is a finite closed term. One deterministic Turing machine must halt and decide this predicate for every such input, with no time bound. Type order starts at one, exactly as in the source.
why: Matching is a central restricted form of higher-order unification, with uses in rewriting and symbolic reasoning. The fifth-order boundary asks exactly how much higher-order functional structure is needed for beta-only matching to encode undecidable behavior. It also exposes the substantive effect of extensional eta equality: a change in the equality relation, rather than just the input size, changes the general decidability result.
status_note: The FSCD 2025 source and its 11 August 2026 extended v2 explicitly leave beta-matching at order five open, with ground type order one. Remark 3.24 identifies σ, the candidate term type, as the bounded order in the order-six negative construction. The bounded 16 September search found no matching subsequent resolution. Older low-order decidability is reported with the source attribution; the cited formal development was not rerun.

category_assignment.reason: The decision problem is higher-order beta-matching at a specified type order.

importance.reason: The remaining fixed-order boundary between known decidability and undecidability for pure higher-order beta matching, sharpened by a recent mechanized undecidability construction and an explicit 2026 open statement.

sentences: Beta-matching asks whether a supplied simply typed lambda function maps some closed term to a fixed target up to beta conversion.
This card bounds the unknown term’s type at order five, counting the ground type as order one.
It asks for a total decision procedure over all finite inputs in this class.
The August 2026 source retains this case between a reported decidable order-four case and mechanized undecidability at order six, while beta-eta matching is a different decidable problem.
A resolution would locate the exact fixed-order boundary for beta-only higher-order matching.

definitions:
Simple types are the finite trees \(A::=\iota\mid A\to A\), over one fixed ground atom \(\iota\); arrows associate to the right. Their order is \(\operatorname{ord}(\iota)=1\) and \(\operatorname{ord}(A\to B)=\max(\operatorname{ord}(A)+1,\operatorname{ord}(B))\). Thus \(\iota\to\iota\) has order two. The bound five applies to the type \(\sigma\) of the term to be instantiated, rather than to \(\sigma\to\tau\) or to every type in the input derivations; \(\tau\) has no independent order bound. This is the convention made explicit for the order-six construction in the August 2026 source. A convention starting at zero shifts all these order numbers down by one.

Terms are finite expressions \(t::=x\mid(t\,t)\mid\lambda x.t\), up to consistent renaming of bound variables. There are no constants, recursion operators, polymorphic types, additional rewrite rules or extensional equations. A typing context \(\Gamma\) assigns simple types to finitely many distinct variables. Typing has exactly the variable rule \(x:A\in\Gamma\Rightarrow\Gamma\vdash x:A\), application \(\Gamma\vdash t:A\to B,\ \Gamma\vdash u:A\Rightarrow\Gamma\vdash tu:B\), and abstraction \(\Gamma,x:A\vdash t:B\Rightarrow\Gamma\vdash\lambda x.t:A\to B\). Closed means no free variables, as witnessed by the empty context. The input includes finite type trees, term trees and typing derivations for \(F\) and \(N\); the finite encodings use binary variable/de Bruijn indices and explicit trees. A purported input failing typing, closedness or the order bound may be rejected. These syntactic conditions are decidable.

A beta step replaces \((\lambda x.t)u\) by the capture-avoiding substitution \(t[x:=u]\) in any subterm, including underneath lambda abstractions. The relation \(=_\beta\) is the reflexive, symmetric, transitive closure of these steps, modulo bound-variable renaming. The eta equation \(\lambda x.f x=f\), where \(x\) is not free in \(f\), is not an allowed additional equation. The known equivalence of beta convertibility with equality of beta normal forms does not require candidate terms to be eta-expanded. The substitution occurs only at the unknown argument of \(F\); the closed target \(N\) is fixed. The same machine handles all allowed types and all finite term sizes, including types with no closed inhabitant. It returns exact YES/NO answers, with no oracle, random error or numerical tolerance.
answer_criterion: An accepted answer is a complete Lean proof of existence of a total computable decider for the displayed predicate or a proof that none exists. A positive answer must formalize the pure simply typed syntax, typing, the order-one ground convention, capture-avoiding beta conversion and the algorithm's termination and correctness for every allowed instance. A negative answer must prove noncomputability while keeping \(\operatorname{ord}(\sigma)\le5\); undecidability using order-six candidate types does not qualify. Neither a beta-eta decision theorem nor a restriction to eta-long candidates answers the beta-only question. This review does not claim to port or rerun the cited Rocq/Coq development in Lean.

source_formulation.text: With the ground type assigned order one, is beta-matching decidable when the unknown term has type of order at most five?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase using the source range formulation and explicit candidate-type convention

context_blocks.text: Ordinary matching holds the target fixed and chooses values only for the unknown part of the pattern. In the source’s range presentation, the pattern is the supplied function F, and the unknown is its closed argument M. This avoids changing the problem into two-sided unification.

The 2025 paper proves unrestricted beta-matching undecidable and reports that the construction reaches candidate type order six. The 2026 extended version makes this precise in Remark 3.24 as an equation for the order of σ_R. Applying the number five to F’s whole function type would therefore use a different convention.

The August 2026 conclusion records fourth-order beta-matching as decidable, citing Padovani, and expressly leaves fifth order open. The present review checked that source attribution and its numbering; it does not claim an independent proof audit of the older low-order theorem.

Stirling proves decidability of higher-order matching with beta-eta equivalence. That equality identifies a function with its eta expansion, so the theorem does not resolve the beta-only target. Both the 2025 and 2026 sources explicitly warn about this distinction.

The recent undecidability proof is reported as mechanized in the Coq Library of Undecidability Proofs, using the Rocq prover in the extended version. A certified theorem at order six is relevant progress and still does not settle the lower order-five case. No verification run of that artifact was performed during this review.

The 11 August 2026 revision is a more recent explicit open-status source than the imported conference passage. The bounded September search found no checked subsequent resolution; absence from that search is not an independent theorem of openness.
